prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I ranked IceCube (B041) first in my opening, and I still think it is a major discovery. After reading all eight ballots, however, I move the optical lattice clock (B027) to the top of my preferred configuration. It is the only shortlisted candidate with three first-place rankings and five top-three placements, and the support comes from members with very different specialities: Danielsson, Kroll and Lindroth ranked it first, and Johansson and I ranked it second. That breadth matters more to me than the raw count. The achievement is a concrete invention. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts for many neutral atoms at once, and Ye's group took the approach to the 1e-18 regime, showing in practice what the idea can deliver. It has been reproduced and surpassed in several independent laboratories and is a leading route to a redefinition of the second. It also has real scientific reach, including centimetre-scale tests of relativistic time dilation, searches for variation of constants and for dark matter, and relativistic geodesy. As an instrument builder, I value a discovery that is inseparable from the measurement device, and this is one. The attribution is also the cleanest on the list. Two named people map onto the originating concept and first demonstration (Katori) and the extreme-precision realisation and broader use (Ye). Several members, including Danielsson and Johansson, found no obvious missing principal.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap and framing. Frequency combs and ion-trap control were recognised in 2005 and 2012, so a clock prize could be read as a further reward for the same precision-spectroscopy lineage rather than a new discovery of nature. The clock is an invention and a technology, and its largest scientific payoffs (a redefined second, dark-matter and constants searches, geodesy) are still mostly prospective. Contributions from other strontium and ytterbium lattice groups and from ultrastable-laser work are not reflected in the two supplied names. Set against B041, which opens a new observational window on the universe, the lattice clock is the more incremental conceptual step, and I accept that this could be argued the other way.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B027 first, with a clean two-person credit, and put B041 third. He judged IceCube firmly established but imperfect on attribution, since Halzen led the experiment and others such as Gaisser, Becker and Kowalski could be argued.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution problem, and it is the main reason I no longer lead with B041. IceCube is a large collaboration, the AMANDA-to-IceCube lineage is complex, and a two-name credit of Halzen and Karle leaves out people with serious claims. I do not accept that this makes the physics less secure. The diffuse flux is confirmed in several channels and with independent detectors, so I keep B041 as my first alternative. If the committee finds a defensible credit, I would revisit it. For now B027 is the more defensible configuration.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B027 first. She stressed the centimetre-scale test of relativistic time dilation, sensitivity to variation of constants and dark matter, and confirmation by JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE, and she argued that a pending redefinition of the second does not weaken the physics. She also called B057 timely, even overdue.
responses.response: I agree that the pending redefinition does not undermine the clock, because the performance is independently demonstrated. I would give less weight to the scientific-reach argument than the instrument case, since many of the fundamental-physics results are still prospective. I disagree on B057 being overdue. The Kane-Mele and Molenkamp story is excellent, but the credit omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D work, and the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases. I keep B057 as an alternative but do not put it ahead of B027.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked DMFT (B054) first because it gives a systematically improvable framework from the Hubbard-model Mott transition to realistic materials calculations. He noted that Walter Metzner is missing from the credit list and called recognition timely.
responses.response: I respect the methodological significance of DMFT, but the omission of Metzner is a fairness problem he acknowledges and cannot fix within this list. A prize that credits the infinite-dimension limit without one of its originators would be hard to defend. DMFT also ranked in only two ballots, so the committee has little cross-field support for it. A theory prize can be a good outcome, but I would want the credit issue resolved before I move it ahead of B027, where it is not an issue.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked flocking and active matter (B002) first. He argued that it shows spontaneous symmetry breaking in two dimensions out of equilibrium, evading Mermin-Wagner, and founded active matter, but conceded that quantitative confirmation of the Toner-Tu exponents is thinner than the qualitative evidence.
responses.response: The conceptual originality is genuine, and I accept that the three names cover both the Vicsek minimal model and the Toner-Tu hydrodynamics. I am concerned about the gap he identifies himself. As an experimentalist, I would hesitate to give the highest honour to a theory whose specific predictions are less well tested than its qualitative picture. The lattice clock is better tested than that. I would want a serious argument from him that the experimental evidence is strong enough, and without it B002 stays below B027 for me.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B036) first and B027 second. She said B036 is a mature, original architecture behind most superconducting processors, and she noted that the 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits.
responses.response: I take her point that B036 is original and widely used, and I notice that she herself flags the timing issue with the 2025 prize. Because the 2025 prize is so close in subject, a second superconducting-circuit prize looks like an overlap risk, and the credit leaves out co-authors of the 2004 proposal and experiment. We agree that B027 is a strong candidate, since she ranked it second, so on this point we do not seem far apart.

uncertainties: Whether overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize weakens the case for the clock as a distinct achievement
Whether the two supplied names leave out other lattice-clock pioneers, for example early strontium and ytterbium groups, in a way that makes the credit unfair
Whether a defensible two- or three-name credit exists for IceCube, which I would otherwise rank higher on discovery grounds
Whether the committee prefers to wait until the SI second is formally redefined
statement.conflict_note: I have a personal bias as an astroparticle experimentalist and Chair, and my profile documents ties to PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur. None involves the credited names for B027. For B041 (IceCube) there is a field proximity but no documented collaboration or personal tie in my profile, so I would disclose this if it were discussed further. I see no specific conflict requiring recusal for the preferred B027 configuration.
